answer: Sybil resistance comes from bonding collateral to each identity and aggregating evidence of coordinated equivocation: when k identities commit correlated faults, the penalty scales as O(k²), not merely with the number of accounts. Detection also triggers an exponential multiplier in capital loss, making a swarm costlier to operate than isolated identities. An island of accounts cannot evade this by splitting stakes; the penalty binds the coordinated set, while asymmetric depreciation makes the loss endure like a relic refracted through a prism.
